summary: The audience is built to feel grief, pity, and awe: dread for Hector, exultation and horror in Achilles' rampage, and tears at Priam's visit.

need-to-breathe.why: Nothing in the poem is built to make the listener feel short of breath.

hungry.why: The feasts are formulaic and not built to make anyone hungry.

full.why: No effect on the audience's satiety.

thirsty.why: No effect on the audience's thirst.

gassy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-poop.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-pee.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

sleepy.why: The poem is for performance and never aims to lull its hearers.

nauseous.why: The wounds are precise rather than sickening; no passage is built to turn the stomach.

urge-to-sneeze.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

urge-to-cough.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

dizzy.why: Nothing is built to produce vertigo.

fatigued.why: The listener is not made to feel bodily exertion, though the battle books are long.

pain.why: The anatomically exact wounds, a spear through the bladder, teeth smashed, brains spattered, are built to make the listener wince.

disgusted.why: Corpses left for dogs and birds, flies kept off Patroclus, and Achilles' wish to eat Hector raw are built to produce revulsion.

itchy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

tickled.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

over-stimulated.why: Nothing is built to assault the listener's senses.

too-hot-too-cold.why: Nothing is built to make the listener feel heat or cold.

afraid.why: Achilles' war cry at the ditch and his blazing pursuit are built to frighten on Hector's behalf, but fear is not the poem's chief aim.

anxious.why: The listener dreads Hector's fate through the farewell at the gate and the long approach of Achilles, dread the poem deliberately prolongs.

panic.why: The routs to the ships and into the river carry some of the crowd's panic to the listener, briefly.

sensory-pleasures.why: Feasts, wine, and the golden cloud on Ida give some vicarious pleasure, but the senses are not the poem's appeal.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: The similes, the catalogue, the shield of Achilles, and the formulaic hexameters are the poem's form, built to delight an audience with language.

piquancy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

fun-excitement.why: Diomedes' aristeia, the chariot race, and the clash of champions are built as thrilling spectacle for the listener.

orgasm.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

love-romantic.why: Hector and Andromache's parting is built to make the listener feel their love, briefly and sharply.

love-family.why: Astyanax shrinking from his father's helmet, Thetis grieving her son, and Priam kissing Achilles' hands are built to move the listener as a parent or child.

grief.why: Achilles' collapse at Patroclus's death and the three laments over Hector are built to draw the listener's own tears; the poem ends on mourning.

missing-someone.why: Patroclus's ghost asking for burial lets the listener feel absence for a moment.

aroused-sexually.why: Hera's seduction of Zeus is told with wit rather than heat; the listener is amused, not aroused.

liking-as-a-friend.why: The listener is built to like Patroclus, Hector, and Nestor, so that their fates land.

empathy.why: The poem gives Trojan and Greek alike their grief and fear, so the listener feels with both sides at once; this even-handedness is its design.

compassion.why: Priam's plea and Achilles' weeping with him are built to produce pity, the poem's last and greatest effect.

grateful.why: Nothing is built to make the listener feel gratitude.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

trustful-distrustful.why: The listener knows Zeus's dream to Agamemnon is false and Deiphobus is Athena, dramatic ironies that make us distrust what the heroes trust.

depressed.why: Nothing is built to make the listener feel unsupported.

angry.why: Agamemnon's seizure of Briseis is built to make the listener share Achilles' anger at the start.

envious.why: Nothing is built to produce envy.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Nothing is built to make the listener jealous.

jealous-friendship.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

hatred.why: The listener is not asked to hate anyone; even Agamemnon and Paris are given their due.

contempt.why: Thersites' beating and Paris's cowardice are built to draw the listener's scorn.

resentment.why: The listener feels the injustice of Agamemnon's theft and of Thersites' unanswered complaint about shares.

proud.why: The listener may share the glow of the heroes' glory, but the poem does not build pride in the audience.

amused.why: The gods' squabbles, Hephaestus limping as cupbearer, and Ajax in the dung are built for laughter between the slaughters.

sense-of-belonging.why: A Greek audience may feel its heroes as its own, but the poem does not work to recruit the listener to a side.

lonely.why: Achilles weeping alone by the sea gives the listener a moment of isolation.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The listener is led to judge Agamemnon's greed, Achilles' excess with Hector's corpse, and Paris's cowardice, while the gods' interventions complicate every verdict.

admiration.why: The poem is built to make the listener admire Hector, Diomedes, Ajax, and Achilles, and Priam's courage above all.

embarrassed.why: Paris's retreat before Menelaus gives the listener a flicker of secondhand embarrassment.

shame.why: The listener may feel Hector's dread of reproach, but is not shamed.

guilt.why: Nothing is built to make the listener feel guilt.

sad.why: The poem's whole last third, from Patroclus's death to Hector's funeral, is built to produce sorrow.

happy.why: Nothing in the poem is built to make the listener content.

joyful-euphoric.why: Achilles' return to battle gives the listener a surge of exultation that the poem quickly darkens.

effort.why: The catalogue of ships, the battle books, and the sheer length demand persistence from a listener or reader.

focused-in-flow.why: The duels and the pursuit of Hector are built to hold the listener in rapt attention.

bored.why: The catalogue of ships and the repetitive battle slaughters can tire a modern reader, though the poem does not aim at boredom.

distracted.why: The digressions and genealogies pull attention sideways, but the poem does not aim to distract.

impatient.why: The listener is made to wait many books for Achilles' return, an impatience the poem builds deliberately.

curious.why: The listener wants to know how the embassy will fare and what Zeus's plan is, but the ending is known from the start.

surprised.why: Priam's sudden appearance in Achilles' tent is built to startle; most events are foretold.

awe.why: The gods fighting among men, Zeus's scales, the shield of Achilles, and the river rising against him are built to produce awe.

skeptical-doubtful.why: The listener is given no reason to doubt the narrator.

feeling-of-knowing.why: Epithets and recurring formulas give the listener recognition rather than the strain of recall.

confused.why: The crowd of names in the catalogue and the battle books can confuse a first-time reader, though not by design.

frustrated.why: Achilles' refusal of the embassy and his long sulk are built to frustrate the listener's wish for his return.

uncertain-certain.why: Zeus's plan is announced, so the listener's uncertainty is confined to how, not whether, each death comes.

understanding.why: Achilles' speech of the two urns is built to give the listener the poem's understanding of mortal grief.

inspired.why: The listener may take the poem's vision of mortality as insight, but it is given, not discovered.

satisfied.why: Hector's ransom and funeral are built to close the wrath that opened the poem, a satisfaction tempered by what is still to come.

foreboding.why: Zeus foretells each death, Thetis and Hector foresee their dooms, and the listener knows Troy will fall; dramatic irony darkens every scene.

nostalgia.why: Nestor's reminiscences and the poem's own distance from a heroic past give the listener a measure of nostalgia.

anticipation-suspense.why: The listener knows Patroclus and Hector will die and waits for it, and Priam's night journey is built as suspense.

hope.why: The listener is allowed to hope the embassy will succeed and that Hector will go inside the walls.

schadenfreude.why: Thersites' beating and Ajax's fall in the dung invite the listener to enjoy a comeuppance.

elevation.why: Priam and Achilles weeping together is built to lift the listener beyond the wrath, the poem's moral summit.

infatuation.why: Paris's desire for Helen is observed, not shared.

rage.why: Achilles' rampage is built to carry the listener along in fury before turning it to horror.
